questions.q: What are the three original Bretton Woods institutions established in 1944, and which one was added later to complete the global economic governance framework?
questions.a: The three original Bretton Woods institutions are the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank), and the planned International Trade Organization (ITO) which failed; the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) served as a provisional substitute until the World Trade Organization (WTO) was established in 1995. A wrong answer (e.g., naming the UN or WTO as original) reveals confusion between the 1944 conference and later institutional developments, and misses how the US used the ITO's failure to maintain unilateral trade leverage until the WTO locked in stronger enforcement.

questions.q: Why does the US have de facto veto power in the IMF and World Bank, and how does this reflect structural power rather than just hard power?
questions.a: The US holds ~16.5% of IMF voting shares and ~15.5% in the World Bank; major decisions require an 85% supermajority, giving the US a de facto veto. This is structural power because it is embedded in the institution's constitutional design (quotas based on economic weight at creation) — not exercised through military force or persuasion. A wrong answer citing "US military pressure" confuses hard power with the baked-in institutional architecture that automatically privileges the hegemon's preferences.

questions.q: A developing country faces a balance-of-payments crisis and approaches the IMF for a loan. The IMF imposes conditionality requiring privatization, fiscal austerity, and capital account liberalization. Explain how this scenario illustrates US structural power, even if US officials are not directly negotiating.
questions.a: The IMF's standard policy template (the "Washington Consensus") reflects US Treasury and Federal Reserve preferences for open markets, deregulation, and creditor rights — embedded in the institution's operational DNA since the 1980s debt crises. The US doesn't need to intervene case-by-case; the rules themselves channel outcomes toward US-favored policies. A wrong answer focusing on "US pressure on the IMF board" misses that structural power works through automated rule-application, not ad hoc intervention.

questions.q: Compare the role of the US dollar as the global reserve currency with the role of the WTO's dispute settlement mechanism. How do both function as instruments of structural power?
questions.a: The dollar's reserve status lets the US borrow cheaply, run persistent deficits, and sanction adversaries by controlling access to dollar-clearing (SWIFT) — an "exorbitant privilege" built into the post-1971 fiat system. The WTO dispute settlement mechanism (pre-2019 appellate body) enforced trade rules largely shaped by US corporate interests (TRIPS, services, agriculture), giving the US a legalized tool to open foreign markets. Both are structural: they operate through systemic rules, not case-by-case coercion. A wrong answer treating them as "US bullying" fails to see how the rules themselves — accepted by all members — structurally advantage the hegemon.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The rise of the BRICS New Development Bank and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank signals the end of US structural power in global finance."
questions.a: The claim overstates the shift. New institutions (NDB, AIIB) challenge the World Bank's monopoly and offer alternatives, but they operate within the dollar system, use IMF-style conditionality, and lack the depth, liquidity, and universal membership of Bretton Woods institutions. US structural power is eroding but not ended — it has shifted from monopoly to "contested hegemony." A wrong answer declaring "US hegemony is over" ignores that structural power persists as long as the dollar, IMF quota system, and WTO rules remain the default framework even for challengers.

questions.q: Draft a 150-word argument for a Model UN position paper: "Reforming the IMF quota formula to reflect current GDP shares would reduce US structural power." Include one specific reform proposal and one reason the US might resist.
questions.a: A strong answer proposes: "Shift to a dynamic quota formula weighted 60% GDP (PPP), 30% trade openness, 10% reserves — recalculated every 5 years." This would cut US share below 15%, removing its veto. The US resists because the veto lets it block policies threatening dollar dominance or creditor interests (e.g., SDR allocations to rivals). A weak answer suggests "give more votes to China" without a formula, or claims the US would accept reform — missing that structural power holders rarely cede institutional privilege voluntarily.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Hegemony as structural power?
questions.a: Students think structural power means the US "controls" the IMF/WTO like a puppet master directing every decision.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how the US uses institutions like the IMF, World Bank, and WTO to embed its preferences into global economic rules, distinguish structural power from hard/soft power with concrete examples, and analyze why emerging powers challenge these institutions while still operating within them.
